name: Chimalapa Zoque
confidence_why: Knudson 1975, Johnson 2000 and Jiménez 2019, three independent first-hand descriptions of San Miguel Chimalapa Zoque, all place primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, and the only difference among them is whether longer words also carry an initial secondary stress, which Knudson reports and the two later grammars do not mention.
catalog_quote: The placement of stress, when predictable, is determined by phonological word boundaries. A phonological word, or simply "word" in this section, in CZ is an utterance of speech involving from one to several syllables which usually is a single grammatical word, but may consist of more than one grammatical word, as in a noun phrase, verb phrase, or a complete clause.

new_statements.quote: El zoque de San Miguel Chimalapa cumple con ambos criterios; esto se puede afirmar dado que la lengua presenta acento fijo en el sentido de que se marca abiertamente en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra; en este sentido, todas las palabras de contenido son acentuadas. (p. 83) [...] Con respecto al patrón acentual, evidencié que la lengua presenta acento tracaico, es decir, el acento se marca en la penúltima sílaba. Además, discutí que la lengua también presenta un paradigma de enclíticos con acento propio que lo conservan cuando éstos se encliticizan a la palabra. (p. 110)
new_statements.translation: San Miguel Chimalapa Zoque meets both criteria [obligatoriness and culminativity]; this can be asserted because the language has fixed stress in the sense that it is overtly marked on the penultimate syllable of the word; in this sense all content words are stressed. (p. 83) [...] As regards the stress pattern, I showed that the language has trochaic stress, that is, stress is marked on the penultimate syllable. I also discussed that the language also has a paradigm of enclitics with their own stress, which they keep when they encliticize to the word. (p. 110)
new_statements.citation: Jiménez Jiménez, Silviano. 2019. Estudios de la gramática de la oración simple y compleja en el zoque de San Miguel Chimalapa. Tesis de doctorado, CIESAS, Ciudad de México. li+1027 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary placement as the catalog (penultimate) and as Johnson 2000 §3.2.1 (already held by the project, HJohnson/ pp. 27-28: 'MIG Zoque words have primary stress on the penultimate syllable'); adds the phonological-word domain (proclitics, enclitics, affixes count), the class of inherently stressed enclitics, and the contraction-derived final stress that Johnson also reports (=/am, -naaN, Spanish loans).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fixed penultimate (trochaic) stress on the phonological word. The domain includes possessor proclitics, the plural enclitic =tɨkaj, case enclitics (comitative =hɨnaŋ, instrumental =piʔt, locative =hoʔ) and affixes (-kuy, -pa, -Wɨ): e.g. [ˈtɨk] 'casa', [ˈtu.ni] 'ciruela', [hu.ˈku.tɨk] 'lumbre', [ko.ˈma.ʃaŋ] 'santo', [pɨn.ˈdɨ.kaj] 'hombres', [mɨ.ʔa.ˈhɨ.naŋ] 'con el venado', [ˈmoŋ.pa] 'duerme'. Monosyllables are stressed. The author notes (p. 880) that stress and stress-attracting clitics still need deeper study.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned; the section discusses only the primary (culminative) stress and never marks or names a secondary stress, so the initial-syllable secondary stress implied by the catalog's StressTyp2 rule string is neither confirmed nor denied here
new_statements.exceptions: A paradigm of enclitics with their own stress pulls stress to the final syllable: [ʔɨn.tɨk.ˈhaʔ] 'nuestras casas' (=haʔ PL), [ʔɨy.jam.tsɨk.pa.ˈnam] 'aún lo recuerda' (=nam), [hu.ho.ˈnaŋ] 'hacia dónde' (=naŋ), [hu.naŋ.ˈxa] 'así como' (=xa), [ʔüy.tuj.xuk.kü.ˈne] (=ne 'también'). Fusion of -tam PL + hortative -'i gives final-stressed [kü.xo.ˈdaŋ] 'comamos'; contraction of =ʔam 'ya' with CP/IP gives ka'ˈwam, ka'ˈpam with stress on the contracted final syllable. Reduced ablative =tɨnaŋ > =tɨŋ keeps stress on the surviving (now final) syllable: [hu.ˈtɨ.naŋ] ~ [hu.ˈtɨŋ].
new_statements.identity_note: Both theses describe the zoque of San Miguel Chimalapa (author's abbreviation ZMIG in 2014, ZMI in 2019), Oaxaca, with data from speakers of four communities in the municipio; Jiménez treats Santa María Chimalapa Zoque as a separate variety and does not describe it. Glottolog chim1300 'Chimalapa Zoque' covers the San Miguel variety, so the statements apply to the catalog item; the StressTyp2 record likely derives from Johnson 2000, which is also San Miguel Chimalapa.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on primary placement: Jiménez 2019 (penultimate, trochaic, phonological-word domain) agrees with Johnson 2000 §3.2.1 (penultimate primary stress; final stress in Spanish loans, contracted forms and the measure suffix -naaN) and with the catalog's StressTyp2 record. One unsupported detail: the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 110 1010 10010 100010 (1 = a stressed syllable) marks a stress on the initial syllable of every word in addition to the penult (i.e. an initial secondary stress), but neither Jiménez 2019 §3.2.4 nor Johnson 2000 ch. 3 (a full-text search for stress/accent over all Johnson text held by the project: no hits) says anything about secondary stress; that initial-syllable component of the catalog rule has no support in the two primary grammars read. Jiménez 2014 is silent.

sources.quote: 'MIG Zoque words have primary stress on the penultimate syllable. Final stress (which will always be marked with an accent in the examples) may arise for one of two reasons: the word is a loan word from Spanish, borrowed with the original stress intact; or, two syllables have been collapsed by a morphophonological rule (section 3.3.8).' No statement on secondary stress anywhere in ch.3 (a full-text search for stress/accent/'first syllable' = 0 hits).
sources.note: Largest English-language reference grammar of the language (San Miguel variety); its sec.3.2.1 independently confirms penultimate primary stress; adds loan/contraction final-stress exceptions; silent on initial secondary stress.
